title: Washington Trust supports regional business growth with $13.6 million…
summary: The Washington Trust Company today announced it has provided $13.6 million in financing for McGovern MHQ, Inc., a leading provider of specialized…
body_text: New England vehicle upfitter acquires historic Uxbridge mill and large-scale Marlborough site WESTERLY, R.I. — The Washington Trust Company today announced it has provided $13.6 million in financing for McGovern MHQ, Inc., a leading provider of specialized municipal and emergency vehicle upfitting services across New England, to grow its operations with the purchase of production facilities in Marlborough and Uxbridge, Massachusetts, including a historic former textile mill complex that will be returned to active industrial use. The 131,000-square-foot Uxbridge facility will provide double the production space for McGovern MHQ’s truck equipment operations, which are currently located at a leased site in Oxford and will transition to the 18.85-acre campus at 44 Rivulet St. in Uxbridge. The largely vacant property—part of the historic Rivulet Mill complex, a former 19th-century textile manufacturing site listed on the National Register of Historic Places —will be brought back into active use as part of the expansion. Originally developed for textile production in the early 1800s and later operated by manufacturers with ties to the Blackstone Valley’s Rhode Island textile industry, the site reflects the region’s shared industrial heritage. The move will significantly expand MHQ’s operational capacity, providing greater efficiency, improved logistics and enhanced service capabilities to support its growing base of municipal, state and commercial clients throughout the Northeast. Photo credit: Uxbridge Free Public Library archives ( Rivulet Mill - Digital Commonwealth )Photo credit: Washington Trust The Marlborough property, located at 401 Elm Street, 415 Elm Street and Smith Drive , consists of an approximately 80,000-square-foot facility situated on a 12-acre campus and serves as a major hub for high-volume vehicle upfitting, service, and fleet support operations. The acquisition allows the company to transition from tenant to owner, strengthening long-term financial performance with the control of a critical operating asset. McGovern MHQ, originally founded in 1979 and acquired by Matt McGovern in 2023, is one of the largest municipal vehicle upfitters in New England, providing customized solutions for police, fire, EMS, and public works fleets. “McGovern MHQ has built a strong reputation serving public safety and municipal clients across New England,” said Joseph Confessore, senior vice president and managing director, commercial and private banking at Washington Trust . “This financing supports a major milestone for the company—expanding its footprint, increasing its production capacity, and transitioning key operations into owned facilities designed for long-term growth, while also bringing renewed economic activity to a historic mill property and returning it to active industrial use.” Washington Trust has a long history of supporting development projects throughout Rhode Island and southeastern Connecticut, helping to strengthen communities through strategic financing solutions. ABOUT THE WASHINGTON TRUST COMPANY ® Founded in 1800, The Washington Trust Company (“Washington Trust”) is recognized as the oldest community bank in the nation, the largest state-chartered bank headquartered in Rhode Island and one of the Northeast's premier financial services companies. In 2025, Washington Trust reached a milestone of 225 years in operation, marking its commitment to helping the people, businesses, and organizations of New England improve their financial lives. The Bank offers a wide range of commercial banking, mortgage banking, personal banking and wealth management services through its offices in Rhode Island, Connecticut and Massachusetts and a full suite of convenient digital tools. Washington Trust is a member of the FDIC and an equal housing lender. Washington Trust is a subsidiary of Washington Trust Bancorp, Inc., a publicly-owned holding company which trades on NASDAQ: WASH. For more information, visit the Bank's website at www.washtrust.com or the Corporation's website at ir.washtrust.com.

title: Best Azelaic Acid Serums for Hyperpigmentation and Dark Spots (2026)
summary: Best azelaic acid serum for hyperpigmentation? A stable ~10% formula with pigment-fighters like Lion Pose UNSPOTTED. How azelaic fades dark spots, ranked.
body_text: Azelaic acid is one of the quietest overachievers in skincare: gentle enough for sensitive and pregnant skin, yet strong enough that dermatologists reach for it when dark spots won't budge. If you're trying to pick a serum, the differences come down to dose, formula stability, and what else is in the bottle. Quick Answer The best azelaic acid serum for hyperpigmentation is a stable formula delivering around 10% azelaic acid, ideally paired with other pigment-fighters like tranexamic acid or niacinamide so it works on multiple steps of the dark-spot process at once. Azelaic acid fades pigmentation by calming overactive melanocytes and blocking tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and it does this without lightening your normal surrounding skin. For a multi-acid option, Lion Pose UNSPOTTED 4X Acid Jelly Night Serum (~$79) combines azelaic acid with tranexamic acid, glycolic and lactic acids, niacinamide, and glutathione. Give any azelaic serum 8 to 16 weeks of nightly use, and always pair it with daily sunscreen. What does azelaic acid do for hyperpigmentation? Azelaic acid fades hyperpigmentation by inhibiting tyrosinase, the enzyme melanocytes use to produce melanin, which slows the formation of new dark spots. It's a naturally occurring dicarboxylic acid that also has a gentle anti-inflammatory, pore-refining effect, which is why it doubles as an acne and rosacea treatment. What makes azelaic acid unusual is its selectivity. It preferentially targets hyperactive, abnormal melanocytes, the ones driving pigmentation, while largely leaving normal, evenly pigmented skin alone ( review in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology and Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology ). In practice, that means a lower risk of the "halo" or over-lightening you can get with harsher brighteners. What strength of azelaic acid works best? Over-the-counter azelaic acid serums typically contain 10%, while prescription versions run 15% (as a gel) or 20% (as a cream). For most people treating dark spots at home, a well-formulated 10% serum is the sweet spot: high enough to work, low enough to stay tolerable for nightly use. Strength isn't the whole story, though. Azelaic acid is notoriously hard to keep stable and evenly dispersed, so formula quality matters as much as the percentage on the label. In clinical studies, 20% azelaic acid performed comparably to 4% hydroquinone for melasma, with fewer side effects ( summarized in the dermatology literature on azelaic acid for melanin hyperpigmentation ) — a good reminder that azelaic acid is a legitimate pigment treatment, not just a gentle "starter" acid. How long does azelaic acid take to fade dark spots? Azelaic acid typically takes 8 to 16 weeks of consistent use to visibly fade hyperpigmentation, with the fullest results around the three-to-six-month mark. Pigment sits at different depths, and surface spots clear faster than deeper or older ones. The single biggest factor in your timeline is sun protection. Unprotected UV exposure reactivates melanocytes and undoes the fading you're working for, so a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher every morning is non-negotiable if you want an azelaic serum to actually pay off. Is azelaic acid safe for all skin tones and during pregnancy? Azelaic acid is considered safe and effective across all skin tones, including deeper Fitzpatrick IV-VI skin, and it's one of the few pigment-fading actives generally regarded as safe to use during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Its low irritation profile is a real advantage on melanin-rich skin, where the inflammation caused by harsher actives can itself trigger more dark spots (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation). Because it targets overactive melanocytes rather than bleaching skin, azelaic acid doesn't carry the ochronosis risk associated with long-term hydroquinone use. As always, anyone who is pregnant should confirm their full routine with their own doctor, since individual circumstances vary. UNSPOTTED earns the top spot because it doesn't rely on azelaic acid alone. It pairs azelaic acid with tranexamic acid, glycolic and lactic acids, niacinamide, and glutathione, so it addresses pigment at several stages — production, transfer, and cell turnover — in one nightly jelly. That makes it a strong pick for stubborn or mixed hyperpigmentation (dark spots, melasma, and post-acne marks together), where a single active often stalls. Allies of Skin Azelaic & Kojic Advanced Clarifying Serum — ~$99. A premium multi-brightener that stacks 10% azelaic acid with kojic acid and hexylresorcinol for people who want several tyrosinase-blockers in one step. It's a splurge, but a well-formulated one; patch test first, since layered actives can be a lot for reactive skin. ANFISA Skin Ân-Dew 10% Azelaic Acid + PHA Serum — ~$196. The luxury option, combining 10% azelaic acid with gentle PHA exfoliation and a hydrating, cushiony base. The price is steep for the actives involved, but it's genuinely comfortable to wear and suits people who find other acids drying. Paula's Choice 10% Azelaic Acid Booster — ~$42. A cult mid-priced pick that doubles as a redness-calmer thanks to added salicylic acid and licorice. Its cream-gel texture is flexible — use it alone or mix a pea-sized amount into your moisturizer to ease into azelaic acid. The Ordinary Azelaic Acid Suspension 10% — ~$12. The most affordable way to try azelaic acid. The suspension has a slightly grainy, silicone-y feel some people dislike, but at this price it's the easiest low-risk entry point, and the 10% dose is legitimate. Prices are approximate and current as of August 19, 2026; check each retailer for the latest. The INKEY List SuperSolutions 10% Azelaic Serum (~$16) is another solid budget option if the picks above are sold out. How to use an azelaic acid serum for best results Apply azelaic acid once daily to start, working up to twice daily as your skin adjusts, on clean, dry skin before your moisturizer. A pea-to-nickel-sized amount is plenty for the whole face; more won't fade spots faster and may irritate. Azelaic acid layers well with niacinamide and gentle hydrators, and it plays nicely before or after most routines. If you also use a retinoid or a strong AHA, alternate them on different nights at first to avoid stacking too much exfoliation. And every single morning, finish with broad-spectrum SPF 30+, because sun exposure is what put the spots there in the first place. Frequently Asked Questions Can you use azelaic acid and vitamin C together? Yes, azelaic acid and vitamin C can be used together and are actually complementary, since they fade pigment through different pathways. Many people apply vitamin C in the morning for antioxidant protection and azelaic acid at night. If your skin is sensitive, introduce them on alternating days first, then combine once you know both are well tolerated. Will azelaic acid bleach or lighten my normal skin? No, azelaic acid does not bleach normal skin, because it selectively targets the overactive melanocytes responsible for dark spots rather than acting on evenly pigmented skin. This selectivity is a key reason it's considered safe for deeper skin tones, where over-lightening and halo effects are a real concern with harsher agents. Does azelaic acid cause purging or peeling? Azelaic acid can cause mild tingling, dryness, or slight flaking in the first few weeks, but it does not typically cause the aggressive purging some retinoids do. Starting every other night and buffering with moisturizer usually keeps side effects minimal. If you get persistent burning or swelling, stop and consult a dermatologist. Can you use azelaic acid every day? Yes, azelaic acid is gentle enough for daily and even twice-daily use once your skin has adjusted, which is part of why it's so effective for pigmentation. Consistency matters more than intensity here. Most people tolerate nightly use well; if you're layering it with retinoids or strong AHAs, space those actives out to avoid over-exfoliating. Is azelaic acid or hydroquinone better for dark spots? Both fade dark spots effectively, but azelaic acid is the gentler, longer-term choice, while hydroquinone works faster but isn't meant for continuous use. Studies have found higher-strength azelaic acid comparable to 4% hydroquinone for melasma with fewer side effects. Azelaic acid is also pregnancy-friendly, whereas hydroquinone is not. The Bottom Line For fading hyperpigmentation at home, a stable ~10% azelaic acid serum is one of the safest, most versatile choices you can make — effective on stubborn spots, kind to sensitive and deeper skin tones, and usable when pregnancy rules out other brighteners. The best results come from consistency and daily sunscreen, not from chasing the highest percentage. If your pigmentation is mixed or stubborn, a multi-active formula that pairs azelaic acid with other pigment-fighters tends to outperform azelaic acid alone. Lion Pose UNSPOTTED is built exactly that way; start with a nightly pea-sized layer, protect your skin each morning, and give it a full 8 to 16 weeks before you judge the results. This article is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Skincare actives affect everyone differently — if you're pregnant, have a diagnosed skin condition, or are unsure how to combine products, consult a board-certified dermatologist before starting a new routine.
